Clustering recipients by address

Source: vignettes/clustering-by-address.Rmd
clustering-by-address.Rmd

One recipient organisation is written many ways across the grant file, and nothing in the filing says which renderings belong together. Grouping them by address is the package’s answer, and it is the same idea in four different places: it collapses the work the cascade has to do, it generates labels no human wrote, it scores a configuration without ground truth, and it supplies the candidate pool for character-level recovery.

This article states the key, what the corpus looks like under it, the four uses as they currently stand, and the ways an address group is not an organisation.

use where what it buys
Identity collapse pf_dedup(), pf_recipients(), pf_propagate_matches() one organisation, one match, propagated to every grant row
Silver labels dev/build-group-index.R, dev/build-triangulation-v2.R, pf_variants the adjudication queue and the bundled variant corpus
A label-free score pf_consistency() within-group EIN agreement, no hand labels required
Reference-side retrieval pf_fuzzy_candidates(), pf_fuzzy_recover() a ZIP5 block as the pool a near-miss name is scored against

1. The key, and why it excludes the name

The group key is the recipient’s normalized street line plus ZIP5 – uppercased alphanumerics of address line 1, then the first five digits of the ZIP:

key <- paste(gsub("[^A-Z0-9]", "", toupper(PF_15_G_PAID_RECIP_ADDR_L1)),
             substr(gsub("[^0-9]", "", PF_15_G_PAID_RECIP_ADDR_ZIP), 1, 5),
             sep = "|")

Address only. The name is never in the key, and that exclusion is the whole point: the name is the thing under test. Because grouping reads only fields the name comparator does not use, a difference between two names inside one group is an observation rather than an assumption, and the groups can be built without matching anything at all.

Two consequences follow from that independence, and both are load-bearing.

Grouping can run over the whole corpus first. It is a chunked scan with no reference, no blocking and no scoring, so the structural question – which addresses carry more than one rendering – is answered for 17.25M rows in about four minutes. Only grants inside a known multi-rendering group need to be matched afterwards. That inverts the original design, which sampled filers, matched them and then looked for groups: 112,806 matched grants yielded 2,853 informative cases, about 40 grants per case, and an organisation funded only by unsampled foundations was invisible however many renderings it had.

A group is evidence about the comparator. If two renderings at one street and ZIP are one organisation, every rendering in the group should receive the same EIN – whatever that EIN turns out to be. That is a check the package can run with no hand labels at all; see section 6.

2. What the corpus looks like under it

Over the deduplicated e-file corpus, efilepf_v3_1, 17,253,199 grant rows:

n
grant rows scanned 17,253,199
distinct address keys 2,326,459
keys with more than one grant 1,380,763
keys with more than one name rendering 596,151
keys with more than one name and more than one year 577,538

So about one address key in four carries more than one way of writing the recipient, and the renderings are stable over time rather than one-off typos: 577,538 of the 596,151 multi-rendering groups span more than one tax year.

Those groups are where most of the grant file lives.
groups 596,151
grant rows inside them 10,586,075 (61.4% of the corpus)
grants per group median 7, mean 17.8, max 19,274
name renderings per group median 2, max 10,363
tax years per group median 5, max 17
grants in group groups grant rows
2 75,861 151,722
3-4 114,848 396,889
5-9 176,448 1,165,969
10-24 142,399 2,123,922
25-99 72,288 3,251,608
100+ 14,307 3,495,965

The distribution is the reason the package batches by identity rather than by row: a handful of enormous groups hold a quarter of the corpus. 14,307 groups of 100 or more grants carry 3.50M grant rows, and the extremes are extreme – one address receives 19,274 grants, and one carries 10,363 distinct renderings. Neither of those is an organisation, which is the subject of the next section.

(dev/GROUP-INDEX.log predates a label fix in dev/build-group-index.R: the run that produced it passed seven labels for six intervals, so the bucket names it prints are shifted by one. The counts are right and are reproduced above against the corrected labels – the arithmetic confirms it, since the “2” bucket holds exactly twice as many grants as groups.)

3. An address group is not an organisation

It is a hypothesis about one, and four populations break it. Each is handled somewhere, and knowing where is the difference between using the clustering and trusting it.

Shared mailboxes. A PO box is a mail convenience, not a shared body. Groups whose street line parses as a box are dropped from the triangulation universe outright (^P?O?BOX|^POST).

Fiscal sponsors and donor-advised-fund custodians. One address legitimately receives grants for hundreds of unrelated projects. The triangulation universe caps a group at fewer than 25 distinct renderings for exactly this reason; the 10,363-rendering address in section 2 is the shape being excluded.

Individuals at an organisation’s address. Scholarship and fellowship payments are filed with the institution’s address and a person’s name. The variant corpus drops a pair if either side has a blank organisation-name line or trips .pf_looks_personal(), which is also why the bundled table ships no individual’s name or home address.

Two organisations in one building. This is the hard one, because nothing about it looks wrong. FIRST PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH and FIRST PRESBYTERIAN FOUNDATION sit at one Boca Raton ZIP and are two EINs. Address line 2 is the only field that bears on it, so pf_street_unit() parses the secondary unit and pf_unit_evidence() turns two parsed units into evidence for a reviewer – different suites at one street is a strong signal of two bodies. It is a prompt for a human, never an automatic verdict.

The residual risk after all four is why the labels in section 5 are silver and why pf_dedup() carries the vetoes in section 4.

4. Use 1 – identity collapse

pf_dedup() is the production use, called by pf_prepare() on every run unless dedup = "none". It turns grant rows into recipient identities at two levels.

Exact. Group by the normalized key (identity_key, street_key, zip5). A hash group-by, linear and safe. This collapses annual repeat grants and the many foundations funding one large charity.

Fuzzy. Cluster the surviving distinct keys – a far smaller set – inside a geographic block: ZIP5 where present, state otherwise, and a record with neither is never clustered. Two names join if their Jaro-Winkler similarity clears threshold (default 0.92), and the accepted joins become single-linkage components by union-find. This absorbs ST JUDES / ST JUDE CHILDRENS RESEARCH HOSP.

g <- pf_dedup(grants, method = "fuzzy", threshold = 0.92)
r <- pf_recipients(g)          # one row per identity, most complete rendering
s <- pf_match_grants(r, ref)   # the cascade runs once per identity
g <- pf_propagate_matches(g, pf_status(s))   # back out to every grant row

What it is worth

The cost saving is real and smaller than expected. Measured as an accumulation curve on the 100k sample, because a single-point measurement understates the full file badly – a 0.8% sample rarely catches two grants to the same recipient:

sample n exact collapse fuzzy collapse
2,000 1.01x 1.02x
10,000 1.03x 1.07x
25,000 1.07x 1.14x
50,000 1.11x 1.21x
98,786 1.17x 1.32x

Fitting log K ~ log n extrapolated to about 1.8x at 12.5M rows. The full-file run came in well above that: 12,559,051 grant rows collapsed to 3,377,452 distinct keys, 3.72x, on method = "exact" alone. No full-file fuzzy figure exists, because the production run used exact dedup. The 1k benchmark collapses 1.03x exact and 1.05x fuzzy, which is why cascade timings taken there understate what dedup is worth at scale.

The recall gain is the better reason to run it. Because a cluster is one organisation by construction, a match found for any member propagates to every member: a truncated, misspelled or acronymic rendering inherits the EIN resolved for an easier rendering in the same cluster. That costs nothing once the clusters exist, and it is the cheapest recall the package has. pf_recipients() leans on the same property in the other direction, choosing the most complete representative of each cluster – longest name, then most address fields populated – so the cascade runs against the best available spelling rather than an arbitrary one.

Batching inherits it too: pf_run_batches() forms batches over recipient_uid, so a cluster is never split across batches and every row of a cluster inherits the one match computed for it.

The trap, and the veto that closes it

The first implementation merged UNIVERSITY OF MASSACHUSETTS AMHERST with UNIVERSITY OF MASSACHUSETTS AMHERST FOUNDATION, and the fuzzy threshold was not the cause. npmatch::np_normalize() strips FOUNDATION as a legal suffix, so the two names are already identical before any comparison happens – exact dedup alone would have merged them. That is correct for matching, where both should be candidates, and wrong for identity, where merging locks one EIN across every row of the cluster. It is also the single most common wrong-but-plausible match in the package: the MAYBE audit found the foundation-versus-operating split in 7 of 100 cases.

So pf_dedup() builds its own identity key from name_full rather than name_key, splitting the suffix list in two. Corporate suffixes – INC, CORP, LLC, LTD – are stripped, since they mark one body in a different wrapper. Affiliate suffixes – FOUNDATION, FUND, TRUST, ASSOCIATION, ENDOWMENT, ALUMNI, FRIENDS – are retained, and a difference in the affiliate-suffix set vetoes a fuzzy join outright:

pair at one address outcome why
AMERICAN HEART ASSOCIATION / … INC merged INC is a corporate wrapper, stripped
DENVER ART MUSEUM / … FOUNDATION held apart affiliate suffix differs - veto
SIERRA CLUB / … FOUNDATION held apart affiliate suffix differs - veto
UNIVERSITY OF MASSACHUSETTS AMHERST / … FOUNDATION held apart affiliate suffix differs - veto

Three further vetoes come from npmatch’s hard predicates: conflicting embedded numbers, ordinals or directions, so LOCAL 32 never merges with LOCAL 45, nor FIRST with SECOND. Inspect what survives with pf_dedup_report(), which prints the cluster-size distribution and the largest clusters – the place over-merging shows up first.

One scaling detail worth knowing, because it changes the result rather than only the runtime: blocks over max_block (2,000) used to be dropped from the fuzzy pass entirely. On the full file roughly 500k of 3.38M keys sit in state-level blocks over that cap, and they are the densest neighbourhoods – exactly where fuzzy matching earns its keep. They are now sub-blocked on the leading characters of the name key, up to three levels deep. Jaro-Winkler weights the common prefix heavily, so splitting on it is close to lossless and bounds the quadratic comparison inside each block.

5. Use 2 – silver labels for cases nobody labelled

The same grouping, run for its evidence rather than its collapse, is where the package’s labels come from. Within one address group, take the best-scoring rendering the cascade cleared YES as the anchor and assign its EIN to the other renderings at that address. That is the triangulation set.

stage n
eligible universe, after the PO-box and fiscal-sponsor filters 504,739 groups / 7,434,953 rows
groups drawn (proportional across size buckets) 36,366
grant rows extracted 540,683
recipient identities matched 91,690
groups still holding 2+ renderings after the match 36,114
groups eligible to label (1+ YES, 1+ non-YES, one YES EIN) 12,474 (34.5%)
informative cases written to the queue 58,680

The 58,680 cases become the adjudication queue and the silver truth file (confidence = "low"). A subset also becomes pf_variants, the bundled corpus of 5,410 anchor/candidate pairs documented in vignette("name-and-address-variants"), restricted to organisation recipients and carrying a name_class taxonomy of what separates the two names.

Two things are worth carrying away from how it was sized. First, the pilot measured yield by group size, and the result is the opposite of the intuition: cases per identity – identities being what the matcher charges for – rise monotonically with group size, so a group of 100+ grants is about eleven times cheaper per case than a group of two.

grants in group eligible cases / group cases / identity
2 28.0% 0.24 0.118
3-4 29.0% 0.36 0.159
5-9 35.2% 0.74 0.274
10-24 35.7% 1.54 0.398
25-99 42.5% 4.66 0.669
100+ 46.0% 15.90 1.283

Buying only the large groups would have delivered 50,000 cases in under two hours, and the set would then be conditioned on the most heavily funded recipients – unreadable as evidence about the comparator’s real failure rate. A proportional draw across the whole universe costs a few more hours and stays representative, so that is what was run.

Second, the label is the assumption under test, not a fact. Assigning the anchor’s EIN to every other rendering at the address is exactly the assumption section 3 lists the exceptions to. So pf_variants sets expected_same_org to TRUE on only 20 rows, where the two names are the same string under a documented cosmetic transformation at an identical address, and NA – never FALSE – on the other 5,390. On 726 rows the candidate’s own match beat the anchor’s, by score or by a stronger pass, which means the silver label is running against the system’s own evidence and should be read before it is trusted.

6. Use 3 – a score that needs no hand labels

pf_consistency() is the address group used as a metric. Within a group, every resolved rendering should carry the same EIN; disagreement is a defect the package can see without anyone adjudicating anything.

pf_consistency(run, groups = "data-dev/TRIANGULATION-GROUPS.csv")
#>   groups with >=2 resolved renderings, EIN agreement, tier-mixed groups, ...

The caveat is section 3 again: a street address also covers fiscal sponsors, individual payees at an organisation’s address, and co-located bodies, so some groups are noisy in every configuration. That does not spoil the comparison it is built for – the groups are fixed, so comparing two configurations on the same groups still isolates the change – but the absolute agreement rate is not a precision figure and should not be quoted as one.

7. Use 4 – the ZIP5 block as a candidate pool

The last use inverts the direction. Sections 4 to 6 group grants with each other; pf_fuzzy_candidates() uses the same geography to pool reference rows around a grant.

Every pass in the cascade is an exact-equality block, so a single mistyped letter in the one distinctive token leaves nothing anywhere to block on, and the correct record is never retrieved – not scored and rejected, never offered:

THE WESMINSTER SCHOOL  (ATLANTA GA 30327) -> THE WESTMINSTER SCHOOLS, 30327
COCORDIA UNIVERSITY    (MEQUON WI 53097)  -> CONCORDIA UNIVERSITY,    53097

Both correct rows sit in the reference at the filed ZIP5. So the recovery is Jaro-Winkler on name_key inside an exact ZIP5 block, with city plus state as a fallback where the ZIP5 block is empty. Blocking first is what makes it affordable: on the 100-case NO sample the pools have a median of 477 reference rows and a maximum of 2,940, against the 223,151 candidates the token pass generates on 5,000 grants.

The cutoff of 0.90 is set from that measurement rather than from taste. It recovers 7 of the 33 identities the BMF does hold and offers exactly one row across the 57 it does not; 0.85 recovers four more, but the highest-scoring personal name sits at 0.848 – ALEXANDER SCHWEIG against ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL ASSOCIATION – and a one-point margin on 38 individuals is not a margin. Jaro-Winkler’s prefix bonus is what rewards a shared first name, so individuals are the population this comparator is worst at excluding, and skip_personal keeps them out of the pool instead of leaving the cutoff to catch them. The whole mechanism, and the three NO cases in 91 it accounts for, is in vignette("outside-the-bmf").

8. What this is not: clustering EINs

One clustering question in this project has a negative answer, and it is easy to confuse with the above. Grouping grant renderings by address is safe because the groups are small, local and structural. Grouping EINs by disclosed affiliation – Schedule A supported organisations, Schedule R related entities – by taking the transitive closure and handing every EIN a cluster_id is not.

566,653 undirected pairs over 174,496 EINs produce a largest connected component of 66,973 EINs across 56 states, 38% of every EIN in the graph, chaining unrelated bodies through intermediaries. A grant “correctly” matched to anything inside it would be unfalsifiable, and geography does not save it: the largest same-city component is still 407 EINs in Phoenix. So the package ships direct edges only – pf_dyads(), a dyad table with no closure and no cluster id – and the union-find it does run is scoped to the candidates inside a single grant, where it cannot chain through an EIN that is not itself a candidate. dev/CLUSTER-FINDINGS.md has the measurement.

The related finding is a reminder that address clustering does not reach everything: 15.9% of the MAYBE tie band is two BMF reference rows carrying one name for one body – JOHNS HOPKINS UNIVERSITY at two EINs, MEMORIAL SLOAN KETTERING CANCER CENTER at two EINs. That is a reference-side problem, and no amount of grant-side grouping touches it.

9. What none of this establishes

Precision. Every number here is about structure and recall. The address group tells you two renderings are probably one organisation; it never tells you the EIN is right. The one measured precision figure in the neighbourhood comes from adjudication, not from clustering.

That the labels are true. Section 5’s labels are silver and unadjudicated by construction, and label_basis in pf_variants records which rows are waiting for a human.

A full-file fuzzy collapse ratio. The production run used exact dedup, so the 1.8x extrapolation and the 3.72x exact measurement are the only two points on record, and they are not comparable.

That the four uses are independent. They are not. The triangulation groups are built from the same addresses pf_dedup() clusters on, so a dedup change moves the labels, which moves pf_consistency(). When comparing configurations, hold the group file fixed – that is why it is written to disk once and reused.

Reproducing 

# the corpus-wide index (chunked scan, no reference needed)
#   Rscript dev/build-group-index.R
#
# the 50,000-case triangulation set, queue and silver truth
#   Rscript dev/build-triangulation-v2.R
#
# the bundled pair corpus
#   Rscript data-raw/make-pf-variants.R
#
# the dedup accumulation curve and the affiliate-suffix guard
#   Rscript dev/measure-dedup.R
